passage:
Irawati, you keep asking why I never sent my story to the college writing contest. Okay. I'm Ritu, and here's the truth.
The story was done by early January. Three thousand words, a proper ending, even a title I liked. All it needed was one last read for typos and the submission form. Maybe an hour.
I didn't do it for five weeks. I told you I was busy. I told myself the ending needed "something." I opened the file twice and closed it without reading.
The contest closed on 10 February. On the 11th I finally read it. It was good. There were four typos. That's all.
What I was actually avoiding was the moment it became real. While it sat at ninety-nine percent, it was a brilliant story in my head. Once I sent it, strangers could say it was bad.
This year, I've put the submission date in my calendar two weeks early. And you're allowed to nag me.

qa.q: How many typos did the story have?
qa.a: There were four typos.

qa.q: What was Ritu really afraid of?
qa.a: Ritu was afraid of judgment, of strangers saying the story was bad once it was submitted.

qa.q: What has Ritu changed for this year, and why might it help?
qa.a: Ritu put the submission date two weeks early in the calendar and asked Irawati to nag, adding a push past the fear.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel hearing this?
qa.a: Irawati might feel sad that the story missed the contest, but glad Ritu is being honest and willing to be nagged.

grounding: Illustrates a student who leaves a nearly finished story unsubmitted for weeks, avoiding the judgment that finishing would bring.

passage:
Hi Kashish,
Before we start on the robotics club's open-day stall, can I suggest something? Last year our stall was "almost ready" for three weeks and still half-built on the day. I think it's because we never said what "done" means.
So here's my draft of done:
1. The line-following robot runs a full lap on the test track three times in a row.
2. The poster is printed, not "on the laptop."
3. The sign-up sheet has a pen tied to it.
4. Both of us have explained the robot out loud to one person who isn't in the club.
When those four are ticked, we stop. No extra features, no "one more tweak." If we have spare time after that, we rest.
Does this list look right to you? Add or cut anything. Once we agree, I'll stick it on the lab door.
Amandeep

qa.q: How many times in a row must the robot run a full lap?
qa.a: Three times in a row.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt about last year's stall?
qa.a: Amandeep probably felt frustrated and a little embarrassed that it was still half-built on the day.

qa.q: Why does writing "done" in advance help the team?
qa.a: It gives clear endpoints like a printed poster and three clean laps, so stopping becomes a decision instead of a drift of endless tweaks.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel reading this email?
qa.a: Kashish would likely feel relieved and included, since the list is clear and open to changes.

grounding: Illustrates a student who writes what finished looks like before starting, so there is no vague ninety percent.

At the city library's community office, Eshaan had spent a week on the new reading-hour flyer for children. It was decent: the time, the place, a drawing of an owl. But he wanted better colours, a second design and maybe a Tamil version.
His colleague Karthik leaned over. "Print fifty of this one. Put them up on Monday. See what the parents say."
"It's not finished."
"It's finished enough to learn from."
Eshaan printed fifty. He put them in the children's section and at two schools nearby.
By Friday, three parents had told the desk the same thing: they couldn't tell if the reading hour was free. Eshaan hadn't thought of that. Two others asked for a Tamil version.
He added "Free, all welcome" in large letters, made the Tamil version and printed the second batch the next Monday.
Twenty-two children came to the first reading hour. Eshaan pinned the first, imperfect flyer above his desk.

qa.q: How many flyers did Eshaan print first?
qa.a: Eshaan printed fifty.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel about printing the flyer before it was perfect?
qa.a: Eshaan felt reluctant and uneasy, believing the flyer was not finished.

qa.q: What did sending out the imperfect version teach Eshaan?
qa.a: Parents' feedback showed the flyer didn't say it was free and that a Tamil version was wanted, things Eshaan hadn't thought of.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel when twenty-two children came?
qa.a: Karthik would likely feel pleased and a little vindicated that printing early worked.

grounding: Illustrates a worker who ships a good-enough flyer, gets feedback and improves it instead of holding it for perfection.

subtype: Attention pulled by whatever is nearby [Actor]
passage:
Lalit sat on the doorstep to put on his chappals. Kamal dada was waiting at the gate to take him to the field.
One chappal went on. Then Lalit saw a shiny green beetle on the step. He poked it with a straw. It walked. He made a little road of pebbles for it.
"Lalit! Chappals!" Kamal dada called.
Lalit looked at his feet. One chappal. One bare foot. He had forgotten.
Dada walked back, smiling, and held out the other chappal. "Beetle can come too?"
Lalit carried the beetle on a leaf all the way to the field.

qa.q: What did Lalit see on the step?
qa.a: A shiny green beetle.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel when he looked at his feet?
qa.a: Lalit felt surprised, having completely forgotten the second chappal while playing with the beetle.

qa.q: How did Kamal dada help Lalit get back on track?
qa.a: Kamal dada called Lalit, came back smiling and handed over the chappal, gently bringing him back to the goal.

qa.q: How might Kamal dada feel watching Lalit with the beetle?
qa.a: Kamal dada seems amused and patient, smiling rather than scolding.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who starts putting on chappals, notices a beetle and forgets the goal until an adult gently reminds him.

subtype: Homework with phone or TV near [Actor]
passage:
The family's one-room house had a single light and a single television, and on Thursday night it was showing the cricket final. Kamal's maths test was the next morning.
He sat on the mat with his notebook, back to the screen. Every roar from the crowd made him turn. Six! He turned. Wicket! He turned. He did one sum, watched an over, then lost his place on the second.
At the drinks break, his big brother Lalit asked, "How many sums?"
"Two." It had been an hour.
Lalit moved Kamal's mat and the lamp to the verandah and pulled the curtain across the door. "Your brain isn't lazy. It just can't ignore a six."
On the verandah, Kamal finished the other eight sums in forty minutes. Lalit told him the final score afterwards.

qa.q: How many sums had Kamal done after an hour?
qa.a: Two.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when each roar came from the television?
qa.a: Kamal felt torn and restless, turning his head at every six and wicket and losing his place in the sums.

qa.q: What did Lalit change that helped, and why?
qa.a: Lalit moved Kamal's mat and lamp to the verandah and pulled the curtain, removing the screen instead of blaming Kamal.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Kamal's distraction?
qa.a: Lalit sees it as normal, not laziness, saying Kamal's brain just can't ignore a six.

grounding: Shows a child doing homework with a cricket match on nearby who keeps glancing at it, until the screen is moved out of view.

passage:
Monday night.
6:10 p.m. I sat down with my biology notes. My phone buzzed. I picked it up to check one message from Pankaj about tomorrow's bus.
6:52 p.m. I looked up and I was watching a video of a man making a sword out of nails. Before that, a dog skateboarding. Before that, I don't know. I don't remember deciding to watch any of it. I never even replied to Pankaj.
Forty minutes. Gone. I felt sick and angry at myself. I always say, "Just one check."
Our science teacher said something last week: these apps are designed so there's no stopping point. Nothing tells you "you're done now." It just keeps going.
So maybe this isn't just me being weak. Maybe I'm fighting something built to win.
Tomorrow the phone goes in Mummy's room while I study. If there's a real message, she can shout.
Ritu

qa.q: What was the video about when the narrator looked up?
qa.a: A man making a sword out of nails.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel after losing forty minutes?
qa.a: Ritu felt sick and angry at the lost time, frustrated with the "just one check" habit.

qa.q: What does Ritu plan for tomorrow, and why is it better than willpower?
qa.a: Putting the phone in Mummy's room while studying, because the apps have no stopping points and willpower alone loses to that design.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel about the unanswered message?
qa.a: Pankaj might feel a bit puzzled or ignored, waiting for a reply about tomorrow's bus.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who picks up the phone for one quick check and surfaces forty minutes later, realising feeds are built to beat willpower.

Evening study time in the girls' hostel ran from seven to nine. Most girls studied on their beds, phones beside them.
Alka didn't. At 6:55 she walked to the warden's desk and put her phone in the small locker the hostel offered, which almost nobody used. Then she went to the study room, not her bed. She took only the chemistry book and one notebook. Her other books stayed in the room.
Her roommate Pallavi followed her the first week, curious. "Don't you get bored without your phone?"
"For the first ten minutes. Then I forget it exists."
"I just tell myself not to look."
"How's that going?"
Pallavi laughed. "I looked eleven times yesterday."
Alka shrugged. "I used to scold myself every night. It never worked. Moving the phone works."
By the second week, Pallavi's phone was in the locker next to Alka's. In the unit test, both of them did better than in the last one.

qa.q: Where did Alka put her phone?
qa.a: In the small locker the hostel offered, at the warden's desk.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel about Alka's routine at first?
qa.a: Pallavi was curious and a little doubtful, asking if Alka got bored without the phone.

qa.q: Why does Alka's method work better than scolding herself?
qa.a: Changing the surroundings removes the pull, with the phone in a locker, a fixed study room and only one book, so there is nothing to resist.

qa.q: How does Pallavi's view change by the second week?
qa.a: Pallavi comes to see that moving the phone works, and puts her own phone in the locker next to Alka's.

grounding: Illustrates a student who puts her phone away, uses a fixed study block and keeps only the needed book, shaping her surroundings instead of scolding herself.

passage:
Dear Minakshi,
You asked how I study so much and still have time to chat. Here's the embarrassing truth: I don't.
Until last week, my "study" looked like this: lecture video playing, two chats open, music in one ear, notes in a doc, and a shopping tab for new shoes. I'd switch every minute. I felt incredibly busy. At the end of three hours, I'd feel tired, like I'd worked hard.
Then we had the economics quiz. I'd "studied" that chapter for two evenings. I got four out of fifteen. I couldn't remember a single graph.
My professor said something about switching: each time you jump to a chat and back, you lose a little, and the losses add up. The tiredness is from switching, not learning.
So this week I tried one tab, no music, forty minutes. It felt slow and boring. But I remembered it the next day.
I'll reply to your messages at nine now, I promise.
Parul

qa.q: What did Parul score in the economics quiz?
qa.a: I got four out of fifteen.

qa.q: How did Parul feel after three hours of multitasking?
qa.a: Parul felt tired and busy, as if a lot of hard work had been done.

qa.q: What change did Parul try, and why does it help?
qa.a: One tab, no music, forty minutes, because it avoids the small losses from switching and lets the learning stick.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Minakshi might feel amused and a little surprised, and perhaps curious to try the same forty-minute focus.

grounding: Illustrates a student who studies with chats, music and videos running, feels busy and retains little, then tries single-task focus.

In the school office, Lakshmi was building next term's timetable, the hardest job of the year. Forty teachers, twenty-two classes, three labs, and a science teacher who could only come after ten. At 11:15 she was finally seeing how the lab slots could fit.
Ping. "Lakshmi, quick question, what's the Wi-Fi password?" It was Usha, from accounts. Lakshmi answered. When she looked back at the grid, the pattern had gone. It took twenty minutes to find it again.
At 12:05, ping: "Which form is for leave?" Then at 12:40: "Is the principal in?"
Each question took one minute to answer. Each time, Lakshmi lost the thread of the timetable for much longer. By lunch she had fixed only two classes.
After lunch she walked over to Usha's desk. "Can we try something? Keep a list of your questions and bring them to me at three. I'm stuck in the timetable till then."
Usha looked surprised. "I thought they were tiny."
"They are. Getting back isn't."

qa.q: How many teachers did the timetable have to cover?
qa.a: Forty teachers.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel each time the pattern disappeared?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt frustrated, losing the thread and needing twenty minutes to find it again after a one-minute question.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi suggest, and why is it a good fix?
qa.a: Lakshmi asked Usha to keep a list and bring questions at three, so the deep work isn't broken again and again.

qa.q: How did Usha see the questions before this conversation?
qa.a: Usha thought they were tiny, not realising how much time Lakshmi lost getting back into the timetable.

grounding: Shows a worker deep in a hard task who is pinged repeatedly with quick questions and loses much more time regaining focus each time.
